insight: Industrialisation and value addition — moving from raw materials to finished goods — is the spine of the economic pillar.
Human capital is a make-or-break: the Human Capital Index of 0.39 is below the regional average and must rise.
Energy is treated as foundational — electricity per person must rise nearly 18-fold to 3,000 kWh.
Almost everything depends on energy: industrialisation, digital services and productivity all assume reliable power.
Delivery depends on skills; a workforce-skills mismatch is named as a persistent challenge.
Trade competitiveness depends on logistics — costs of 35-45% of imports are among the world's highest.
R&D is underfunded; the plan sets a floor of 1% of GDP, implying today's spend is below it.
A narrow tax base (11.9% tax-to-GDP) limits domestic financing for the Vision.
Low electricity access and per-capita use constrain industry, especially in rural areas.
Regulatory complexity, overlapping levies and bureaucracy raise the cost of doing business and logistics.
Limited access to affordable financing slows energy, R&D and enterprise investment.
Brain drain and skills shortages threaten research and innovation capacity.
The Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project (2,115 MW) is a near-term lever to unlock industrial power.
A youthful population (43% under 15) is a demographic dividend if skilled and employed.
Critical minerals position Tanzania in global energy-transition supply chains.
Gateway geography plus AfCFTA make Tanzania a natural regional trade and logistics hub.
Weak execution: the plan itself warns it will not tolerate weak implementation of past plans.
Aid dependency; the framework pushes PPPs and domestic savings to reduce reliance on external funding.
Growth that is not inclusive — prior growth 'lacked inclusivity' and did not cut poverty enough.
Climate change threatens agriculture, water and infrastructure across the plan.
